a: For it is we who are
p: One pronoun: Paul writes that 'we' are God's temple, or that 'you' are. The KJV has 'you.'

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: For it is we who are

readings.w: The Byzantine majority text and the Textus Receptus (KJV 'ye are'); also the reading of 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 6:19 ('you are')
readings.plain: For it is you who are

why: Every modern critical edition prints 'we.' A copyist is much more likely to change 'we' to 'you' than the reverse, because the verses around (6:14, 17; 7:1) speak to 'you,' and because 1 Corinthians 3:16 says 'you are God's temple.' Paul's 'we' is meant to include himself and the Corinthians.
b: The sense barely changes. The plural 'we' includes both Paul and his readers. 'You' makes the verse match 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 6:19 exactly, and it matches the 'you' of the verses around it. The quotation that follows also has a small difference ('my people' in the critical text against 'to me a people' in the Byzantine and TR), which does not change the English.

p: Tregelles reads the simple past eschen ('had') where the other editions have the perfect eschēken ('has had').

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine majority text
Tregelles

why: The Plain follows the editions that agree. The two tenses give the same English.

a: I see that this letter grieved you
t: Is 'for' part of the text at 7:8?
p: The word gar ('for') is present in the NA28, the Tyndale House text, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text, and absent from the SBLGNT. The Plain leaves it out.

readings.w: SBLGNT (no gar)
readings.plain: I see that this letter grieved you

readings.w: NA28, Tyndale House GNT, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont)
readings.plain: for I see that this letter grieved you

why: The Plain follows the SBLGNT, which has no gar. The connecting word adds almost nothing in English, and the sentence reads smoothly without it.
b: The site's word data marks the word as present in NA28, Tyndale House, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text, and absent from the SBLGNT.

p: One verb, with or without a prefix. The English is the same; the KJV has 'worketh.'

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
the Byzantine majority text and the Textus Receptus (KJV 'worketh')

why: The Plain follows the editions with the shorter verb. The prefix kat- only strengthens the verb, and the second half of the verse already has the longer form (katergazetai, 'produces death').
b: No difference in meaning; the contrast between the two griefs is the same.

t: 'Your eagerness for us' or 'our eagerness for you'?
p: Whose eagerness is made plain: the Corinthians' for Paul, or Paul's for the Corinthians? The KJV's wording ('our care for you') matches the second.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT and the Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont). The site's word data lists no pronoun difference at 7:12 in any edition, the Textus Receptus included
readings.orig: τὴν σπουδὴν ὑμῶν τὴν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν

readings.w: The KJV's wording, 'our care for you.' The site's word data lists no pronoun difference in any edition, so it does not show which Greek text the KJV followed here
readings.orig: τὴν σπουδὴν ἡμῶν τὴν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν

why: The Plain follows the Greek in the site's word data, where the critical and Byzantine texts agree: 'your eagerness for us.' On this reading the Corinthians' own eagerness is the point, which fits 7:11; the KJV's wording makes Paul's care the point.
b: The two wordings give the severe letter a different point. On the first reading Paul wrote to test the church's loyalty to him, and the test showed its eagerness. On the KJV's wording he wrote so that his own care for them would be visible 'in the sight of God.'

p: Paul says the news comforted him, or that the Corinthians were comforted. The KJV follows the second.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
the Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and the Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV 'in your comfort')

why: The critical text has 'our comfort': Paul's own comfort is what he has just described (7:6-7, 13a) and Titus's joy is added to it. 'Your comfort' would make the sentence mean that Paul rejoiced over the comfort the Corinthians received, which is possible but less natural after 'this is why we have been comforted.'
b: Again a one-pronoun change. In 7:13 the Plain's meaning is that Paul found comfort, and then even more joy in how Titus was refreshed by the Corinthians.

p: Two Greek words for 'beyond' stand in the editions. The English is the same.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
the Byzantine majority text and the Textus Receptus

why: The Plain follows the critical text. Both prepositions mean 'beyond' here, and one could easily replace the other.

a: the grace of sharing in the service to the saints
t: Did the Macedonians beg Paul to take the gift?
p: The Textus Receptus adds words that make the Macedonians ask Paul to 'receive' the gift. The oldest manuscripts lack them.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, and the Byzantine majority text
readings.orig: τὴν χάριν καὶ τὴν κοινωνίαν τῆς διακονίας τῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους
readings.en: the grace and the sharing of the service to the saints
readings.plain: the grace of sharing in the service to the saints

readings.w: The Textus Receptus (KJV 'that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship')
readings.plain: the grace of sharing in the service to the saints, and that we receive it

why: The Plain follows the critical text. The added words (dexasthai hēmas, 'that we receive it') appear in the Textus Receptus but not in the Byzantine majority text or in the critical editions, and they read like help for the unusual 'grace and fellowship.'
b: The KJV reading makes Paul the one who agrees to take the gift on. The critical text has the Macedonians begging for the privilege of taking part, which is the more striking image: the poor insisting on giving.

a: the love that is in you from us
t: 'The love from us in you' or 'your love in us'?
p: A one-letter difference: the love Paul stirred in the Corinthians, or the love they have for Paul. The KJV has the second.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: τῇ ἐξ ἡμῶν ἐν ὑμῖν ἀγάπῃ
readings.en: the love from us in you
readings.plain: the love that is in you from us

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, the Byzantine majority text and the Textus Receptus (KJV 'your love to us')
readings.orig: τῇ ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐν ἡμῖν ἀγάπῃ
readings.en: the love from you in us
readings.plain: the love that is in us from you

why: The Plain follows NA28 and SBLGNT. The wording 'the love from us in you' is the harder of the two and is the sort of phrase a copyist would turn into the smoother 'your love for us.' Editors are divided: the Tyndale House text prints the other reading.
b: On the critical text the love that the Corinthians have is itself something Paul brought into being, which fits his habit of calling himself their father (1 Corinthians 4:15). On the other reading, the love is the Corinthians' love for Paul and for the apostles, and 'overflow in this grace' is the test of it.

p: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus add tis ('anyone') after 'has' (KJV 'a man hath').

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
the Byzantine majority text and the Textus Receptus

why: The Plain follows the critical text. The subject is understood either way, so the English has 'a person' in both readings.
b: No change to the meaning; the extra word only states the subject.

p: One tense: God who gave the eagerness (a completed act), or who gives it (a continuing one). The first is in the NA28.

readings.w: NA28
SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, the Byzantine majority text and the Textus Receptus

why: The Plain follows the NA28: the simple past fits Paul's thanks for what has already happened in Titus. The editions are split, and the sense for the reader hardly changes.
b: The continuing tense would stress that God keeps working in Titus; the past tense points to the moment Titus took up the task.

p: The Textus Receptus reads 'your' where the other editions read 'our' (KJV 'declaration of your ready mind').

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles and the Byzantine majority text
the Textus Receptus (KJV 'your ready mind')

why: The Plain follows every edition but the Textus Receptus. 'Our readiness' fits the line before it: the brother travels to help Paul's group carry out the gift. 'Your readiness' would turn the sentence toward the Corinthians' eagerness, which 8:11 and 9:2 already praise.
b: A second small difference: the preposition before 'this grace' is syn ('with') in NA28, SBLGNT, the Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text, and en ('in') in the Tyndale House text, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles. 'Traveling companion in carrying out this grace' fits either.

a: We plan ahead for what is good
p: The oldest text has a full verb with 'for'; the Textus Receptus has a participle that hangs on 8:20 (KJV 'providing for honest things').

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: for we plan for good things
readings.plain: We plan ahead for what is good

readings.w: the Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and the Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV 'Providing for honest things')
readings.plain: Planning ahead for what is good

why: The Plain follows the critical text. A participle 'providing' reads smoothly after 8:20 ('avoiding... providing'), which is why a copyist might have changed the harder full verb with 'for.' The sense is the same either way.
b: The quotation behind both is Proverbs 3:4 in the Greek Old Testament, which Paul also echoes in Romans 12:17.

p: The Byzantine text, Textus Receptus, Tyndale House GNT and Westcott-Hort have an imperative ('show'). The NA28, SBLGNT and Tregelles have a participle ('showing').

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tregelles
Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, the Byzantine majority text and the Textus Receptus (KJV 'shew ye')

why: The Plain gives a command. That is what the participle means if it is read as an order, as Paul's participles often are in his closing instructions (compare Romans 12:9-13), and it is what the other reading says outright. The base text (SBLGNT) has the participle, so this entry marks that the English is the same for both.
b: If the participle is not taken as a command, it can join 8:23 and mean 'by showing them the proof...' The sense is not changed.

p: The critical text has to hymōn zēlos (a neuter article before 'your zeal'); the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus have ho ex hymōn zēlos ('the zeal from you').

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
the Byzantine majority text and the Textus Receptus (KJV 'your zeal')

why: The Plain follows the critical text. Its article is neuter beside the noun zēlos, an unusual pairing, which makes it the harder reading; a copyist could have smoothed it into 'the zeal from you.' The English is the same.

p: The KJV ends the verse with 'confident boasting.' The critical text stops at 'confidence.'

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
the Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and the Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV 'in this same confident boasting')
readings.orig: ἐν τῇ ὑποστάσει ταύτῃ τῆς καυχήσεως
readings.plain: over this very confidence of boasting

why: The Plain follows the critical text. The words 'of boasting' look like a copyist's gloss that spells out what the rare word hypostasis ('confidence, assurance, undertaking') means here, with 'boasting' taken from 9:3. A small further difference is in the verb of '(not to speak of you)': NA28 and NA27 have legō ('I say'), the other editions legōmen ('we say'); the sense is the same.
b: Hypostasis can also mean 'undertaking, project' (so 'this project'), which is how some translators take it.

p: The oldest Greek says the gift was promised in advance; the Textus Receptus says it was announced in advance (KJV 'whereof ye had notice before').

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
the Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and the Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV 'whereof ye had notice before')
readings.plain: the gift that was announced beforehand

why: The Plain follows the critical text. Paul's word 'promised' ties to 9:2 and 8:10-11, where the Corinthians had committed themselves a year earlier. 'Announced beforehand' makes the gift something Paul had told others about, which the context also says; the two words differ by a prefix and are easy to confuse.
b: Tregelles reads a different preposition before 'you' (pros for eis), which does not change the English.

a: what he has decided in his heart
p: The tense of the verb changes whether the gift was settled beforehand or is decided by each giver as he gives.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: as he has purposed in the heart
readings.plain: what he has decided in his heart

readings.w: the Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and the Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV 'as he purposeth in his heart')
readings.en: as he purposes in the heart
readings.plain: what he decides in his heart

why: The Plain follows the critical text, a perfect tense: each giver has already made up his mind. A copyist could easily change a rare perfect form into the common present. The sense for the reader is nearly the same; the perfect leans toward a settled decision, in line with Paul's wish that the gift be ready before he comes (9:5).
b: The KJV's 'purposeth' is a present tense.

a: will provide the seed you sow and multiply it, and will make the fruits of your righteousness grow
p: In the oldest text Paul promises that God 'will' supply and multiply. In the Textus Receptus the same verbs are a wish: 'may he supply.'

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: will supply and will multiply... will increase
readings.plain: will provide the seed you sow and multiply it, and will make the fruits of your righteousness grow

readings.w: the Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and the Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV) (KJV 'both minister bread... and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits')
readings.en: may he supply and multiply... increase
readings.plain: may provide the seed you sow and multiply it, and may make the fruits of your righteousness grow

why: The Plain follows the critical text, which has plain futures. The second reading uses a rare form (the optative, a wish) and runs the verse on from 9:8-9 as a prayer. The earlier text gives Paul's confident promise; it is about the harvest of righteousness and not about money (see the notes on 9:6).
b: A second small difference: the word for 'seed' (sporos in NA28, SBLGNT, Treg; sperma in the Tyndale House text, Westcott-Hort, TR and Byzantine) means the same thing in English.
